claims.text: Applying a nanostructured oxide nanocomposite coating to CoCrFeNi will induce an adaptive, self-healing tribofilm during sliding.
The coating will reduce both friction and wear consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi exhibits variable friction and elevated wear across the stated temperature range because of uncontrolled oxidation and mechanical degradation.
Pre-engineering the coating's thickness, phase distribution, and oxidation kinetics will promote a controlled reaction during sliding.
The engineered surface layer will evolve under sliding into an adaptive, lubricious tribofilm.
At lower temperatures, the coating will retain its integrity and resist wear by limiting uncontrolled oxidation.
Increasing sliding speed and associated frictional heating raises surface temperature and promotes thermal softening and oxidation.
At higher temperatures, controlled oxidation of the coating will form a continuous, self-healing glaze layer.
An oxide glaze layer can provide solid lubrication and lead to a gentler wear regime.
The proposed glaze layer will lower interfacial shear stress in coated CoCrFeNi.
The coating will compensate for the mechanical degradation experienced by unmodified CoCrFeNi at high temperature.
Relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, coated samples will have a lower and more stable coefficient of friction and lower wear rates throughout the full temperature range.
The adaptive oxide tribofilm will mitigate both adhesive wear and oxidative wear.
Oxide-layer cracking, plastic deformation, and thermal softening can increase friction and wear under high loads, speeds, or temperatures.
The intervention will remain effective in air from room temperature to 800 °C over practical ranges of normal load and sliding speed.
Performance outside the specified temperature range or in substantially different environments such as inert atmospheres is unverified.
Coating oxidation kinetics and mechanical integrity may be sensitive to variable loads, rapid temperature changes, composition, and microstructure.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant reduction in both friction and wear over the entire tested range, or failure to form an intact adaptive tribofilm, would falsify the hypothesis.
